title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters
theme: Real progress comes from creating something new that no one else offers, and the best businesses do this so well that they escape competition altogether.
summary: Zero to One grew out of a course on startups that Peter Thiel taught at Stanford, with student Blake Masters turning his class notes into the book. Its core distinction is between two kinds of progress. Copying what already works and spreading it more widely takes the world from one to many. Inventing something genuinely new takes it from zero to one. Thiel argues that the future depends on the second kind, and that it rarely happens by accident.
He urges founders to look for important truths that most people do not yet accept. Such hidden truths, which he calls secrets, are where new companies begin.

His most provocative claim is that competition is bad for business. In crowded markets, firms fight over thin margins and have no room to plan for the long term. Lasting value comes from a creative monopoly: a company so much better at something that rivals cannot easily follow. Thiel lists the features such firms tend to share: proprietary technology far better than the alternatives, network effects, economies of scale and a strong brand.

To build one, a startup should first dominate a small, specific market and then expand outward, rather than chase a huge market where it is a minor player. Being the last company to make a great leap in a market matters more than being the first to enter it.

Thiel also stresses that success follows a power law: a few outcomes dwarf all the rest, so investors and founders should concentrate on the few bets that could matter most. He warns that mistakes in a company's founding team and ownership are very hard to fix later, and that selling and distribution deserve as much attention as the product.
The book ends by asking founders to plan deliberately for a definite future instead of trusting luck.
takeaway: Build something truly new, start by owning a small market, and plan deliberately rather than compete head-on for crumbs.

questions.q: What does 'going from zero to one' mean in the book?
options: Expanding an existing business into new countries
Creating something genuinely new that did not exist before
Cutting costs to beat competitors
Raising a company's first round of funding
questions.why: Thiel contrasts vertical progress, inventing the new, with horizontal progress, copying what already works.

questions.q: Going 'from one to n' refers mainly to:
options: Copying and spreading things that already work
Building a monopoly
Founding a company with one partner
Inventing a breakthrough technology
questions.why: Horizontal progress multiplies existing models, as globalization spreads proven ideas.

questions.q: What is Thiel's view of intense competition between firms?
options: It is the main source of innovation
It is necessary for all profitable businesses
It erodes profits and leaves no room for long-term planning
It matters only in technology industries
questions.why: He argues that competitive markets drive margins toward zero and trap firms in short-term survival.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the monopoly features Thiel describes?
options: Network effects
Economies of scale
Proprietary technology
Being first to enter a market
questions.why: Thiel downplays first-mover status and stresses the last decisive move instead.

questions.q: How does Thiel suggest a startup should choose its first market?
options: Dominate a small, specific market, then expand
Target the largest market available
Enter where competitors are weakest on price
Launch in every market at once
questions.why: A small market can be owned outright, giving a base from which to grow into adjacent ones.

questions.q: In the book, a 'secret' is best described as:
options: Confidential company data
A patent filing
An important truth that few people yet recognise
A trade technique kept from employees
questions.why: Thiel urges founders to find unrecognised truths, since these are where new businesses begin.

questions.q: What does the 'power law' imply for investors and founders?
options: Returns are spread evenly across many bets
A small number of outcomes produce most of the value
Diversification removes all risk
Large companies always beat startups
questions.why: Because a few winners outweigh everything else, attention should go to the bets that could matter most.

questions.q: Why does Thiel emphasise getting a company's foundations right?
options: Investors only read founding documents
Founding teams are easy to replace later
Legal rules forbid later changes
Mistakes in the founding team and ownership are very hard to fix later
questions.why: He holds that a startup with flawed foundations usually cannot be repaired afterwards.

questions.q: What does Thiel say about sales and distribution?
options: They deserve as much attention as building the product
A great product sells itself
They should be outsourced
They matter only for consumer products
questions.why: He argues that many good products fail because founders neglect how they will reach customers.

questions.q: Which attitude toward the future does the book favour?
options: Trusting that things will improve by themselves
Avoiding long-term plans because the future is unknowable
Waiting for markets to signal the right moment
Making deliberate, concrete plans to shape the future
questions.why: Thiel prefers definite optimism, building a specific future by design rather than relying on luck.
